claim: A well-orchestrated interplay of three interneuron types shapes the development and refinement of negative prediction-error neurons in a computational model of mouse primary visual cortex.
source: Here, we show that a well-orchestrated interplay of three interneuron types shapes the development and refinement of negative prediction-error neurons in a computational model of mouse primary visual cortex.
evidence: The abstract directly states this as a main finding of the computational modeling study.

claim: Experience-dependent inhibitory plasticity can generate different variants of prediction-error circuits by balancing excitation and inhibition in multiple pathways.
source: By balancing excitation and inhibition in multiple pathways, experience-dependent inhibitory plasticity can generate different variants of prediction-error circuits, which can be distinguished by simulated optogenetic experiments.
evidence: The abstract states this as a finding from the computational model.

claim: Different variants of prediction-error circuits can be distinguished by simulated optogenetic experiments.
source: By balancing excitation and inhibition in multiple pathways, experience-dependent inhibitory plasticity can generate different variants of prediction-error circuits, which can be distinguished by simulated optogenetic experiments.
evidence: The abstract states this as a prediction from the computational model.

claim: The experience-dependence of the model circuit is consistent with that of negative prediction-error circuits in layer 2/3 of mouse primary visual cortex.
source: The experience-dependence of the model circuit is consistent with that of negative prediction-error circuits in layer 2/3 of mouse primary visual cortex.
evidence: The abstract states this as a comparison between model results and experimental data.

claim: Perceptual systems subtract from sensory data an internal prediction calculated from an efference copy of motor signals.
source: A common assumption is that perceptual systems subtract from the sensory data an internal prediction (Bell, 1981; Rao and Ballard, 1999; Friston, 2005; Spratling, 2010; Franklin and Wolpert, 2011; den Ouden et al., 2012; Kennedy et al., 2014; Keller and Mrsic-Flogel, 2018), which is calculated from an efference copy of the motor signals our brain has issued.
evidence: The statement is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Changes in the external world take the form of mismatches between internal predictions and sensory data.
source: Changes in the external world then take the form of mismatches – or prediction errors – between internal predictions and sensory data (Wolpert et al., 1995).
evidence: The statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Dopaminergic neurons in the basal ganglia and the striatum encode a reward prediction error.
source: Dopaminergic neurons in the basal ganglia and the striatum (Schultz and Dickinson, 2000) encode a reward prediction error (mismatch between expected and received reward), and subsets of neurons in visual cortex (Keller et al., 2012; Zmarz and Keller, 2016; Attinger et al., 2017), auditory cortex (Eliades and Wang, 2008; Keller and Hahnloser, 2009) and barrel cortex (Ayaz et al., 2019) code for a mismatch between feedback and feedforward information.
evidence: The statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Subsets of neurons in visual cortex, auditory cortex and barrel cortex code for a mismatch between feedback and feedforward information.
source: Dopaminergic neurons in the basal ganglia and the striatum (Schultz and Dickinson, 2000) encode a reward prediction error (mismatch between expected and received reward), and subsets of neurons in visual cortex (Keller et al., 2012; Zmarz and Keller, 2016; Attinger et al., 2017), auditory cortex (Eliades and Wang, 2008; Keller and Hahnloser, 2009) and barrel cortex (Ayaz et al., 2019) code for a mismatch between feedback and feedforward information.
evidence: The statement is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Negative prediction-error neurons are likely to receive excitatory predictions counterbalanced by inhibitory sensory signals.
source: Negative prediction-error (nPE) neurons, which are activated only when sensory signals are weaker than predicted, are likely to receive excitatory predictions counterbalanced by inhibitory sensory signals.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis based on the computational requirements of prediction errors.

claim: Positive prediction-error neurons may receive excitatory sensory signals counterbalanced by inhibitory predictions.
source: Conversely, positive prediction-error (pPE) neurons, which respond only when sensory signals exceed the internal prediction, may receive excitatory sensory signals counterbalanced by inhibitory predictions (Rao and Ballard, 1999; Keller and Mrsic-Flogel, 2018).
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The network model includes excitatory pyramidal cells and inhibitory parvalbumin-expressing, somatostatin-expressing and vasoactive intestinal peptide-expressing interneurons.
source: The network model includes excitatory pyramidal cells (PCs) as well as inhibitory parvalbumin-expressing (PV), somatostatin-expressing (SOM) and vasoactive intestinal peptide-expressing (VIP) interneurons (Figure 1a).
evidence: The manuscript describes the model architecture and references Figure 1a.

claim: The relative abundance of the four cell types and the probability of the respective synaptic connections are chosen in line with electrophysiological studies.
source: The relative abundance of the four cell types and the probability of the respective synaptic connections are chosen in line with electrophysiological studies (see Materials and methods).
evidence: The manuscript states that model parameters are based on experimental data.

claim: A two-compartment model for pyramidal cells was used with a rectifying active dendritic process that allowed nonlinear dynamics akin to dendritic calcium spikes.
source: While all inhibitory neurons are modeled as point neurons (Wilson and Cowan, 1972), we used a two-compartment model for PCs with a rectifying active dendritic process that allowed nonlinear dynamics akin to dendritic calcium spikes (Murayama et al., 2009) (see Materials and methods and Appendix 1).
evidence: The manuscript describes the modeling approach with citations to prior work.

claim: Before plasticity, all pyramidal cells change their firing rate in response to both feedback and playback stimuli, indicating the absence of nPE neurons.
source: Before the onset of plasticity, synaptic connections were randomly initialized, leading to PCs receiving unbalanced excitation and inhibition. Therefore, all PCs change their firing rate in response to both feedback and playback stimuli, indicating the absence of nPE neurons (Figure 1c).
evidence: The manuscript describes the initial state of the model before learning and references Figure 1c.

claim: After synaptic plasticity, somatic excitation and inhibition are balanced on a stimulus-by-stimulus basis.
source: After synaptic plasticity, somatic excitation and inhibition are balanced on a stimulus-by-stimulus basis (Figure 1d–e).
evidence: The manuscript describes the state after learning and references Figure 1d-e.

claim: After plasticity, all pyramidal cells show an increase in activity for feedback mismatch stimuli.
source: In contrast, all PCs show an increase in activity for feedback mismatch stimuli (Figure 1d), which scales with the size of the difference between actual and predicted visual input (Figure 1e).
evidence: The manuscript describes the model results after learning and references Figure 1d and 1e.

claim: The mismatch response scales with the size of the difference between actual and predicted visual input.
source: In contrast, all PCs show an increase in activity for feedback mismatch stimuli (Figure 1d), which scales with the size of the difference between actual and predicted visual input (Figure 1e).
evidence: The manuscript describes the model results and references Figure 1e.

claim: Inhibitory synaptic plasticity generates nPE neurons by balancing excitation and inhibition in PCs for quasi-natural conditions.
source: Hence, inhibitory synaptic plasticity generates nPE neurons by balancing excitation and inhibition in PCs for quasi-natural conditions.
evidence: The manuscript states this as a conclusion from the modeling results.

claim: Pyramidal cells and SOM and PV interneurons show visual responses.
source: The circuit we studied so far was motivated by the widely accepted view that PCs and SOM and PV interneurons show visual responses (Ko et al., 2011; Yang et al., 2013; Larkum, 2013a; Xue et al., 2014; Harris and Shepherd, 2015; Lee et al., 2016; Attinger et al., 2017), while long-range (motor) predictions arrive in the superficial layers of V1 and target VIP neurons (Fu et al., 2014; Harris and Shepherd, 2015; Tremblay et al., 2016; Attinger et al., 2017) and the apical and distal compartments of PCs (Larkum, 2013a; Leinweber et al., 2017; Attinger et al., 2017).
evidence: The statement is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Long-range motor predictions arrive in the superficial layers of V1 and target VIP neurons and the apical and distal compartments of PCs.
source: The circuit we studied so far was motivated by the widely accepted view that PCs and SOM and PV interneurons show visual responses (Ko et al., 2011; Yang et al., 2013; Larkum, 2013a; Xue et al., 2014; Harris and Shepherd, 2015; Lee et al., 2016; Attinger et al., 2017), while long-range (motor) predictions arrive in the superficial layers of V1 and target VIP neurons (Fu et al., 2014; Harris and Shepherd, 2015; Tremblay et al., 2016; Attinger et al., 2017) and the apical and distal compartments of PCs (Larkum, 2013a; Leinweber et al., 2017; Attinger et al., 2017).
evidence: The statement is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Inhibitory plasticity establishes nPE neurons independent of the input configuration onto PCs and PV neurons.
source: We found that inhibitory plasticity establishes nPE neurons independent of the input configuration onto PCs and PV neurons (Figure 2c–f, right).
evidence: The manuscript describes the model results and references Figure 2c-f.

claim: For PCs not to respond above baseline in feedback and playback phase, various excitatory, inhibitory, disinhibitory and dis-disinhibitory pathways need to be balanced.
source: For PCs not to respond above baseline in feedback and playback phase, various excitatory, inhibitory, disinhibitory and dis-disinhibitory pathways need to be balanced.
evidence: The manuscript states this as a requirement derived from the model analysis.

claim: PV neuron activity reflects whether PCs receive visual input.
source: PV neuron activity reflects whether PCs receive visual input: If PCs receive visual input, PV responses increase during feedback and playback phases to balance the sensory input at the soma of PCs (Figure 2c–d, right). If PCs receive no visual input, PV neurons remain at their baseline firing rate (Figure 2e–f, right), which is in contradiction to the experimentally observed increase of PV neurons during feedback (see Attinger et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript describes the model results and references Figure 2c-f, and compares with experimental data.

claim: If PCs receive visual input, PV responses increase during feedback and playback phases to balance the sensory input at the soma of PCs.
source: PV neuron activity reflects whether PCs receive visual input: If PCs receive visual input, PV responses increase during feedback and playback phases to balance the sensory input at the soma of PCs (Figure 2c–d, right).
evidence: The manuscript describes the model results and references Figure 2c-d.

claim: If PCs receive no visual input, PV neurons remain at their baseline firing rate, which is in contradiction to the experimentally observed increase of PV neurons during feedback.
source: If PCs receive no visual input, PV neurons remain at their baseline firing rate (Figure 2e–f, right), which is in contradiction to the experimentally observed increase of PV neurons during feedback (see Attinger et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript describes the model results, references Figure 2e-f, and compares with experimental data.

claim: The activity of SOM and VIP neurons varies between playback, feedback and mismatch phases in line with experimental results.
source: The activity of SOM and VIP neurons varies between playback, feedback and mismatch phases (in line with experimental results, see Attinger et al., 2017), but is independent of the input configuration for PCs and PV interneurons (Figure 2c–f, right).
evidence: The manuscript describes the model results, references Figure 2c-f, and compares with experimental data.

claim: Simulated optogenetic experiments are highly informative about the underlying input configuration.
source: We found that in our model, such simulated optogenetic experiments are highly informative about the underlying input configuration (Figure 3).
evidence: The manuscript describes the model results and references Figure 3.

claim: PV neuron inactivation changes the response of nPE neurons during feedback, playback and mismatch phases if and only if the PCs receive visual inputs.
source: For example, PV neuron inactivation changes the response of nPE neurons during feedback, playback and mismatch phases if and only if the PCs receive visual inputs.
evidence: The manuscript describes the model results from simulated optogenetic experiments.

claim: VIP inactivation renders nPE neurons silent unless PV neurons receive motor predictions, in which case they are transformed into positive prediction-error neurons.
source: VIP inactivation renders nPE neurons silent unless PV neurons receive motor predictions, in which case they are transformed into positive prediction-error (pPE) neurons.
evidence: The manuscript describes the model results from simulated optogenetic experiments.

claim: A homogeneous input configuration in which all PCs receive visual input while all PV neurons receive a motor-related prediction thereof is unlikely based on comparison with optogenetic experiments.
source: When we compared our results with optogenetic experiments in which SOM or VIP neurons are either inactivated or activated during mismatch or running (Attinger et al., 2017), it shows that a homogeneous input configuration in which all PCs receive visual input while all PV neurons receive a motor-related prediction thereof is unlikely (Figure 3b).
evidence: The manuscript compares model results with experimental data and references Figure 3b.

claim: The fraction of PCs that develop into nPE neurons depends on the distribution of visual and motor input onto SOM and VIP neurons.
source: Given that in our model, motor predictions arriving at the apical dendrites are canceled by SOM neuron-mediated inhibition, we hypothesized that the fraction of PCs that develop into nPE neurons depends on the distribution of visual and motor input onto SOM and VIP neurons.
evidence: The manuscript states this as a hypothesis tested in the model.

claim: Reducing the proportion of SOM neurons that receive visual input decreases the fraction of nPE neurons.
source: Reducing the proportion of SOM neurons that receive visual input (and, equivalently, the proportion of VIP neurons that receive the motor prediction), the fraction of nPE neurons decreases (Figure 4b, middle).
evidence: The manuscript describes the model results and references Figure 4b.

claim: Positive prediction-error neurons only emerge when the inputs to SOM and VIP neurons are reversed such that most SOM neurons receive motor predictions.
source: pPE neurons only emerge when the inputs to SOM and VIP neurons are reversed such that most SOM neurons receive motor predictions (Figure 4b, right).
evidence: The manuscript describes the model results and references Figure 4b.

claim: The number of nPE neurons and the strength of their mismatch responses decreases when mice are trained in artificial conditions during which motor predictions and visual flow were uncorrelated.
source: Attinger et al., 2017 showed that the number of nPE neurons and the strength of their mismatch responses decreases when mice are trained in artificial conditions, during which a mouse was shown the visual information of a different mouse, such that motor predictions and visual flow were uncorrelated ('non-coupled training').
evidence: The manuscript cites experimental findings from Attinger et al., 2017.

claim: The number of nPE neurons and their mismatch responses decrease for random gain trained relative to quasi-natural trained networks in the model.
source: We found that the number of nPE neurons and their mismatch responses also decrease for random gain trained relative to quasi-natural trained networks (Figure 5b).
evidence: The manuscript describes the model results and references Figure 5b.

claim: The decrease in nPE neurons with random gain training is primarily due to changes in PCs and PV neurons, while the responses of SOM and VIP neurons during the mismatch phase are largely independent of the training paradigm.
source: This decrease is primarily due to changes in PCs and PV neurons, while the responses of SOM and VIP neurons during the mismatch phase are largely independent of the training paradigm (Figure 5c).
evidence: The manuscript describes the model results and references Figure 5c.

claim: The experience-dependence of the model circuit is in line with that of nPE neurons in rodent V1.
source: Hence, the experience-dependence of the model circuit is in line with that of nPE neurons in rodent V1 (Attinger et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript compares model results with experimental data.

claim: In mouse V1, nPE neurons exhibit an average rate decrease during playback when the animals were only exposed to perfectly coupled sensorimotor experience.
source: In mouse V1, nPE neurons exhibit an average rate decrease during playback when the animals were only exposed to perfectly coupled sensorimotor experience (Attinger et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites experimental findings from Attinger et al., 2017.

claim: When the network was trained with perfectly coupled sensorimotor experience, PCs reduced their firing rate during playback phases.
source: When our network was trained in the same way, we also observed that PCs reduced their firing rate during playback phases (Figure 5d and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript describes the model results and references Figure 5d and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The model predicts that the rate reduction during playback phases observed by Attinger et al., 2017 vanishes when playback phases are included during training.
source: The model hence predicts that the rate reduction during playback phases observed by Attinger et al., 2017 vanishes when playback phases are included during training.
evidence: The manuscript states this as a prediction from the model.

claim: nPE neurons also emerged when the backpropagation rules were replaced by a form of plasticity that changes SOM→PV and VIP→PV synapses in proportion to the difference between the excitatory recurrent drive onto PV neurons and a target value.
source: We found that nPE neurons also emerged when the backpropagation rules were replaced by a form of plasticity that changes SOM→PV and VIP→PV synapses in proportion to the difference between the excitatory recurrent drive onto PV neurons and a target value (see Mackwood et al., 2020, and Equations 17 and 18 in Materials and methods).
evidence: The manuscript describes alternative plasticity rules that also produce nPE neurons.

claim: The backpropagation-like learning rules for the synapses onto PV neurons can be approximated by biologically plausible rules that exploit local information available at the respective synapses.
source: In summary, the backpropagation-like learning rules for the synapses onto PV neurons can be approximated by biologically plausible rules that exploit local information available at the respective synapses.
evidence: The manuscript states this as a conclusion from testing alternative plasticity rules.

claim: The multi-pathway balance of excitation and inhibition suggests that the input configuration of the prediction circuit could be disambiguated using cell type-specific modulations of neural activity.
source: Firstly, the multi-pathway balance of excitation and inhibition suggests that the input configuration of the prediction circuit could be disambiguated using cell type-specific modulations of neural activity.
evidence: The manuscript states this as a prediction from the model.

claim: The model predicts that sensorimotor experience an animal is habituated to should lead to balanced excitation and inhibition in PCs.
source: It therefore predicts that (i) sensorimotor experience an animal is habituated to should lead to balanced excitation and inhibition in PCs, (ii) E/I balance should break for sensorimotor experience the animal has rarely encountered, for example for mismatches of sensory stimuli and motor predictions and (iii) during altered sensorimotor experience in a virtual reality setting or when the excitability of specific interneuron types is altered, interneuron circuits should gradually reconfigure to reestablish the E/I balance.
evidence: The manuscript states this as a prediction from the model.

claim: The model predicts that E/I balance should break for sensorimotor experience the animal has rarely encountered.
source: It therefore predicts that (i) sensorimotor experience an animal is habituated to should lead to balanced excitation and inhibition in PCs, (ii) E/I balance should break for sensorimotor experience the animal has rarely encountered, for example for mismatches of sensory stimuli and motor predictions and (iii) during altered sensorimotor experience in a virtual reality setting or when the excitability of specific interneuron types is altered, interneuron circuits should gradually reconfigure to reestablish the E/I balance.
evidence: The manuscript states this as a prediction from the model.

claim: The model predicts that during altered sensorimotor experience, interneuron circuits should gradually reconfigure to reestablish the E/I balance.
source: It therefore predicts that (i) sensorimotor experience an animal is habituated to should lead to balanced excitation and inhibition in PCs, (ii) E/I balance should break for sensorimotor experience the animal has rarely encountered, for example for mismatches of sensory stimuli and motor predictions and (iii) during altered sensorimotor experience in a virtual reality setting or when the excitability of specific interneuron types is altered, interneuron circuits should gradually reconfigure to reestablish the E/I balance.
evidence: The manuscript states this as a prediction from the model.

claim: PCs in L2/3 of V1 have very low spontaneous firing rates.
source: PCs in L2/3 of V1 have very low spontaneous firing rates (Polack et al., 2013; Xue et al., 2014).
evidence: The statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: VIP→PV synapses are required for a perfect E/I balance during both feedback and playback phases.
source: In addition to the connections between interneuron classes that are frequently reported as strong and numerous, we included VIP→PV synapses in the circuit, because a mathematical analysis reveals that they are required for a perfect E/I balance during both feedback and playback phases (see Appendix 1).
evidence: The manuscript states this as a result from mathematical analysis.

claim: VIP→PV synapses have been found in visual, auditory, somatosensory and medial prefrontal cortex, as well as amygdala.
source: While VIP→PV synapses have been found in visual (Pfeffer et al., 2013), auditory (Pi et al., 2013), somatosensory (Hioki et al., 2013; Lee et al., 2013) and medial prefrontal cortex (Pi et al., 2013), as well as amygdala (Krabbe et al., 2019), they are less prominent and often weaker than SOM→PV connections (but see Krabbe et al., 2019).
evidence: The statement is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: VIP→PV synapses can be excluded when the conditions for nPE neurons during feedback and playback phases are mildly relaxed and when PV neurons receive visual, but not motor inputs.
source: VIP→PV synapses can be excluded when the conditions for nPE neurons during feedback and playback phases are mildly relaxed (Keller and Hahnloser, 2009; Keller et al., 2012; Attinger et al., 2017) and when PV neurons receive visual, but not motor inputs (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript describes conditions under which VIP→PV synapses are not required, with citations and reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: NDNF neurons unspecifically inhibit apical dendrites located in the superficial layers, and at the same time receive strong inhibition from SOM neurons.
source: In particular, NDNF neurons unspecifically inhibit apical dendrites located in the superficial layers, and at the same time receive strong inhibition from SOM neurons (Abs et al., 2018).
evidence: The statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The assumption that mainly the inhibitory synapses onto PV neurons are plastic is supported by the observation that PV neuron activity is experience-dependent.
source: However, the assumption that mainly the inhibitory synapses onto PV neurons are plastic is supported by the observation that PV neuron activity – in contrast to SOM and VIP neuron activity – is experience-dependent (Attinger et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript justifies a modeling choice by citing experimental observations.

claim: nPE neurons can also develop in a network in which the excitatory top-down and bottom-up connections undergo experience-dependent plasticity that balances excitation and inhibition in somatic and dendritic compartments of PCs.
source: As a matter of fact, nPE neurons can also develop in a network, in which the excitatory top-down and bottom-up connections undergo experience-dependent plasticity that balances excitation and inhibition in somatic and dendritic compartments of PCs.
evidence: The manuscript describes an alternative model configuration.

claim: The firing rate dynamics of each interneuron is modeled by a rectified, linear differential equation.
source: The firing rate dynamics of each interneuron is modeled by a rectified, linear differential equation (Wilson and Cowan, 1972),
evidence: The manuscript describes the model equations with a citation.

claim: PCs are defined as nPE neurons when they exclusively increase their firing rate during feedback mismatch while remaining at their baseline during feedback and playback phases.
source: We define PCs as nPE neurons when they exclusively increase their firing rate during feedback mismatch (visual input smaller than predicted), while remaining at their baseline during feedback and playback phases.
evidence: The manuscript defines the classification criteria for nPE neurons.

claim: All neurons receive constant, external background input that ensures reasonable baseline firing rates in the absence of visual and motor-related input.
source: All neurons receive constant, external background input that ensures reasonable baseline firing rates in the absence of visual and motor-related input.
evidence: The manuscript describes the model inputs.

claim: The connections from PV and SOM neurons onto the soma and the apical dendrites obey inhibitory Hebbian plasticity rules akin to Vogels et al., 2011.
source: In detail, the connections from PV and SOM neurons onto the soma and the apical dendrites, respectively, obey inhibitory Hebbian plasticity rules akin to Vogels et al., 2011
evidence: The manuscript describes the plasticity rules with a citation.

claim: The connections from both SOM and VIP neurons onto PV neurons implement an approximation of a backpropagation of error.
source: The connections from both SOM and VIP neurons onto PV neurons implement an approximation of a backpropagation of error
evidence: The manuscript describes the plasticity rules.

claim: All simulations were performed in customized Python code.
source: All simulations were performed in customized Python code written by LH.
evidence: The manuscript describes the implementation details.

claim: Differential equations were numerically integrated using a 2nd-order Runge-Kutta method with time steps between 0.05 and 2 ms.
source: Differential equations were numerically integrated using a 2nd-order Runge-Kutta method with time steps between 0.05 and 2 ms.
evidence: The manuscript describes the numerical methods.
